title: Greek sailors and Celtic chiefs: Marseille and the Celts
story: Imagine a bay on the Mediterranean coast, around 600 BC. A Greek ship from Phocaea, in today's Turkey, drops anchor. Its captain meets a local chief, and the legend says that the chief's daughter chooses the stranger as her husband. A few miles inland, Celtic horsemen watch the sails with curiosity. Two worlds are about to meet.
objective: I can say who founded Marseille and when, who the Celts were, and what each group brought.

write.heading: 1. Marseille, the oldest city
write.body: Around **600 BC**, Greeks from **Phocaea** found **Massalia** (today's **Marseille**), the oldest city in France. They come by sea to trade. Legend says the Greek Protis married Gyptis, daughter of a local chief. Like the farmers of Carnac, these settlers choose a coast with good land (→ L3).

write.heading: 2. What the Greeks bring
write.body:
- **Vines** and **olive trees**: wine and oil.
- **Coins** and **writing** (the Greek alphabet).
- A city with its own laws, trading all round the Mediterranean.

write.heading: 3. The Celts
write.body: The **Celts** are a group of peoples who share a language and customs. They spread over Europe from the **8th century BC**. They make iron tools and weapons, so we call the period the **Iron Age**. Their rich culture is called **La Tène** (from about **450 BC**). The Romans will call the Celts of our land the **Gauls** (→ L1).

write.heading: 4. A princess of Vix
write.body: Around **500 BC**, a Celtic princess is buried at **Vix**, in Burgundy, with a bronze vase **1.64 m** tall, made in a Greek workshop. It proves that Greeks and Celts traded.

check.q: Who founded Massalia, and around when?
check.a: Greek sailors from Phocaea, around 600 BC.

check.q: Name three things the Greeks brought to Gaul.
check.a: Vines, olive trees, coins and writing (any three).

check.q: What did the tomb of Vix prove?
check.a: That Celts and Greeks traded: a Greek-made vase lay in a Celtic tomb.

read_more: The Vix vase, found in 1953, is the largest known bronze vase of the ancient world. It is shown at the museum of Châtillon-sur-Seine. Marseille still celebrates its Greek birth: it is often called "the Phocaean city" (la cité phocéenne), and its football team is Olympique de Marseille.
